 Election 2026: Early voting wraps for Tennessee’s November 3 general election 
 The early voting period is over, and Tennessee’s state and federal general election is on November 3. 
 By Caleb Wethington Published : Oct. 14, 2026 at 9:18 AM CDT | Updated : 17 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google What This Story Is About 
 Tennessee voters will head to the polls Tuesday, Nov. 3, to choose a governor, U.S. senator, members of Congress, state lawmakers, and, in some communities, municipal officials. 
 Why It Matters 
 The general election will decide who holds those offices, with Republican, Democratic and Independent candidates appearing on ballots. 
 What Happens Next 
 Election Day is November 3. 
 Catch Up 
 2026 Election: These 3 changes could be coming to the Tennessee Constitution. Here’s what to know. 
 NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - Early voting for Tennesseans officially ended, and now voters will cast ballots in the State and Federal General Election on Tuesday, November 3.
 Races on the ballot include governor, U.S. Senate, U.S. House, Tennessee Senate and Tennessee House seats. Some cities and counties will also have local races.
 This comprehensive voter’s guide outlines the candidates, their platforms, who will be on each ballot, who can vote in a primary election, the difference between a primary and a general election, how to vote and a timeline of important dates. 
 Get live election results here as they come in on November 3.
 What are the key dates and deadlines for Tennessee’s upcoming elections? 
 Here are the deadlines for the November 3 State and Federal Election , which includes the following races:
 Governor 
 U.S. Senate 
 U.S. House 
 Tennessee Senate (odd-numbered districts) 
 Tennessee House 
 Some municipal elections 
 Deadline Date 
 Voter Registration Deadline Monday, October 5, 2026 
 Early Voting Wednesday, October 14 - Thursday, October 29, 2026 
 Absentee Ballot Request Deadline Saturday, October 24, 2026 
 Election Day Tuesday, November 3, 2026 
 What do you need to vote in Tennessee? 
 The state has an online hub called GoVoteTN.gov to help voters get to the polls on Election Day. The hub is also available as a free mobile app. 
 Only registered voters can cast a ballot. Tennessee voters must bring a valid photo ID to the polls. The state accepts a Tennessee driver’s license, a state-issued photo ID or a federal government-issued photo ID, including an expired ID.
 Voters can use the state’s GoVoteTN website or mobile app to register, check their registration, find their polling location, locate their county election commission and track an absentee ballot.

 Which proposed amendments will be on Tennessee ballots this November? 
 Amendment No. 1: 
 According to a summary provided by the Tennessee Secretary of State, this amendment, if passed, would allow courts to hold defendants without bail before trial in certain circumstances. This would be a change to Article I, Section 15 of the state constitution and would require that courts state the reasons for the decision on the record.
 If passed, bail would be withheld before trial in the following cases:
 An offense punishable by the death penalty 
 An act of terrorism 
 Second-degree murder 
 Aggravated rape of a child 
 Aggravated rape 
 Grave torture 
 Any crime for which a convicted person would be required to serve 85% of their sentence 
 Here’s how the proposal will appear on the ballot: 
 Shall Article I, Section 15 of the Constitution of Tennessee be amended by deleting the following:
 That all prisoners shall be bailable by sufficient sureties, unless for capital offences, when the proof is evident, or the presumption great. And the privilege of the writ of Habeas Corpus shall not be suspended, unless when in case of rebellion or invasion, the General Assembly shall declare the public safety requires it.
 and substituting instead the following:
 (a) All prisoners shall be bailable by sufficient sureties unless for the following when the proof is evident or the presumption great:
 (1) A capital offense;
 (2) An act of terrorism;
 (3) Second degree murder;
 (4) Aggravated rape of a child;
 (5) Aggravated rape;
 (6) Grave torture; and
 (7) Any other offense for which, as of November 3, 2026, a defendant, if convicted, could not be released prior to the expiration of at least eighty-five percent of the entire sentence imposed.
 (b) In any case in which bail for an offense listed in subsection (a) is granted or denied before conviction, the judge or magistrate shall place in the record the judge’s or magistrate’s reasons for granting or denying bail.
 (c) The privilege of the writ of Habeas Corpus shall not be suspended, unless when in case of rebellion or invasion, the General Assembly shall declare the public safety requires it.
 ☐ Yes
 ☐ No
 Read more about the amendment HERE and HERE .
 Amendment No. 2: 
 A state summary says that, if passed, this amendment would ban the Tennessee Legislature from imposing a state property tax on real, personal or mixed property. This would affect Article II, section 28 of the state constitution.
 Tennessee does not currently have a state property tax, although local governments do have the ability to set their own rates.
 Here’s how the proposal will appear on the ballot: 
 Shall Article II, Section 28 of the Constitution of the State of Tennessee be amended by deleting the following language from the first sentence:
 In accordance with the following provisions, all property real, personal or mixed shall be subject to taxation, but the Legislature
 and substituting instead the following:
 In accordance with the following provisions, all property real, personal, or mixed shall be subject to taxation, but the Legislature shall not levy, authorize, or otherwise permit any state tax upon such property, and the Legislature
 ☐ Yes
 ☐ No
 Read more about the amendment HERE and HERE .
 Amendment No. 3: 
 The state says that, if approved by voters, this amendment would help clarify and add rights for crime victims, under Article I, section 35 of the state constitution.
 New rights include:
 Fair treatment 
 To be informed about and participate in the parole process 
 Harassment, intimidation and abuse protection 
 To be informed about the minimum sentence the convicted criminal will serve and their scheduled release 
 To have their safety, their family’s safety and the public’s safety taken into account before a convicted criminal is released 
 Clarified rights include:
 To be informed about legal proceedings involving the criminal and be present about proceedings that are public 
 To be informed of any release, transfer or escape of the criminal 
 To talk to prosecutors and make statements about the conviction, sentencing or release process 
 Speedy resolution of the case 
 Restitution from the convicted criminal 
 To be informed of their rights 
 Here’s how the proposal will appear on the ballot: 
 Shall Article I, Section 35 of the Constitution of Tennessee be amended by deleting the section in its entirety and substituting the following:
 Section 35. That to preserve and protect the rights of victims of crime to justice and due process throughout the criminal and juvenile justice systems, a victim, as defined by law and which may be expanded by the General Assembly, shall have the following rights, which shall be protected:
 (1) The right to be treated with fairness for the victim’s safety and dignity;
 (2) The right, upon request, to reasonable notice of all public criminal proceedings and all public juvenile delinquency proceedings involving the accused;
 (3) The right to be present at all public criminal proceedings and all public juvenile delinquency proceedings involving the accused;
 (4) The right upon request to be heard in any proceeding involving release, plea, sentencing, disposition, and parole, as well as any public proceeding when relevant during which a right of the victim is implicated;
 (5) The right to be heard and informed of all parole procedures, to participate in the parole process, to provide information to the parole authority to be considered before the parole of the offender, and to be notified, upon request, of the parole or other release of the offender;
 (6) The right to be free from harassment, intimidation, and abuse throughout the criminal justice system, including reasonable protection, as defined by the General Assembly, from the accused or any person acting on behalf of the accused;
 (7) The right, upon request, to reasonable notice of any release, transfer, or escape of the accused or convicted person;
 (8) The right to full and timely restitution from the offender;
 (9) The right to a speedy trial or disposition and a prompt and final conclusion of the case after the conviction or sentence;
 (10) The right to be informed of the minimum sentence the offender will serve in custody and the scheduled release date;
 (11) The right to have the safety of the victim, the victim’s family, and the general public considered before any parole or other post-judgment release decision is made;
 (12) The right, upon request, to confer with the prosecution; and
 (13) The right to be fully informed of all rights afforded to crime victims.
 A victim may assert the rights enumerated in this section, not as a party, but in the manner further provided by the General Assembly protecting the victim’s right to standing. The General Assembly has the authority to enact substantive and procedural laws to further define, implement, preserve, and protect the rights guaranteed to victims by this section. This section must be interpreted to preserve and protect the rights of all persons to due process. This section, or any law enacted under this section, does not create a basis for vacating a conviction. This section does not restrict the powers of the District Attorney General or the inherent authority of the court.
 Other than as provided in the preceding paragraph, this section does not create a cause of action or claim for damages against the state or a political subdivision of the state; an officer, employee, or agent of the state or of any of its political subdivisions; or an officer or employee of the court.
 ☐ Yes
 ☐ No
 Read more about the amendment HERE and HERE .
 Here’s how amendment voting works in Tennessee 
 The amendments will appear on the ballot directly after the candidates for governor. If you vote “yes,” that means you want to pass the amendment and for the Tennessee Constitution to be amended. If you vote “no,” you want to keep the state constitution as-is.
 In order for an amendment to be officially passed, it must receive more “yes” votes than “no,” and the number of “yes” votes must be more than half of all votes cast in the governor’s race.
 What is the difference between the Primary Election and the General Election? 
 A primary election selects the Republican and Democratic candidates for a general election , so it comes first in a voting cycle. 
 Primary elections are all about political party affiliations. The goal of a primary is for voters to narrow down the pool of candidates representing each major political party, so that heading into the general election, there is one Republican and one Democrat for each race. Independents are not included in primaries. 
 Candidates run in a primary election with the goal of winning their party’s race. Winning a primary means voters have nominated that candidate to represent their party in the general election. 
 A general election features a myriad of candidates. Some of those candidates are ones who won their primary race, and others only appear in the general election. 
 The U.S. Vote Foundation says the following offices fall under the umbrella of a general election:
 Elected federal officials are U.S. Senators and U.S. Representatives to Congress. 
 Elected state officials are governor, lieutenant governor, general assembly, attorney general, auditor general and state treasurer. 
 Elected local officials are county and city officials, judges and magisterial district judges.
